lesson.menu_desc: Reading model -- chairing a call in three cities: dial in, loop in, chime in, talk over, cut out, hand over, park, on the same page, takeaway, consensus -- and question tags: isn't it?, didn't we?, can't he? -- 29 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 28 -- Multi-Party Calls -- Three Cities, One Call
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Simone Quiles de Santana Marques | Lesson 28 -- Multi-Party Calls
lesson.grammar_point: question tags to check agreement on a call (isn't it / don't we / didn't we / can't he)

listenings.text: Simone, it is Lucia. Thank you for agreeing to chair tomorrow's call. Here is who is dialing in. From Madrid, Javier and me. From New York, Ryan, and he is looping in Tom Walsh from the tax side. And from Sao Paulo, Paulo Mendes, our local counsel. That is five people in three cities, plus you, so it will not be easy. Last time, Ryan and Javier talked over each other for ten minutes, and nobody remembers what we decided. So, three things. First, open with the agenda: the new date, the indemnity and the documents. Second, if the interest question gets complicated, park it and come back to it at the end. Tom will want to discuss it for an hour. Third, before you close, check that everyone is on the same page, and send the takeaways in writing the same day. If we have consensus on the date and the indemnity, that is a good call.

Hi Simone, it is Tom Walsh, from the tax side in New York. Thank you for chairing this morning. Honestly, it was the most efficient call we have had on this deal. Before you send the summary, I want to check my notes, because I cut out for a minute in the middle. We agreed on the fifteenth of April for the closing, didn't we? And the indemnity covers the full tax debt. The interest is the one point we parked, and you said we would come back to it on Thursday, didn't you? Paulo is going to send the documents by Friday. If that is correct, then I am on the same page. One small request: next time, can you hand over to me a little earlier? I almost chimed in twice, and I did not want to talk over Javier. Thanks again.

extra_audio.text: First, before the call, you send the agenda and you check who will dial in. Then, you open the call: you welcome everyone and you say the three points. After that, you hand over to each person by name, and you park any topic that is too big. Next, you check agreement with question tags, like we agreed on April, didn't we? Finally, you close with the takeaways, and you send them in writing the same day.

reading.rtitle: Why Calls with Five People Go Wrong
paras: A meeting in a room has rules that nobody needs to explain. People see who wants to speak, they see who is confused, and they wait for a pause. On a call with five people in three cities, all of that disappears. Somebody cuts out, two people talk over each other, and the most senior person speaks for twenty minutes while the others check their email.

The solution is not more technology. It is a chair: one person who manages the turns. A good chair opens the call with the agenda and the takeaway everyone needs at the end. Then she hands over to each person by name, instead of asking: does anyone have anything to add? On a call, that question usually gets silence.

Two small tools help a lot. The first is the question tag. A sentence like we agreed on April, didn't we? checks agreement and passes the turn at the same time. The second is the parking lot. When a topic is too big for the call, the chair parks it, writes it down, and comes back to it at the end, so it does not take over the whole call.

Finally, a call is only finished when everyone is on the same page. The chair summarizes the decisions, checks for consensus, and loops in anyone who was not there. Then she sends the takeaways in writing within the hour. A call without a written summary is a call that will happen again.

reading.prompt: Read once, quickly. Which title fits the whole text best?
choices: Calls with many people need better technology and faster internet connections in every office
A multi-party call works when one chair manages the turns, parks big topics and checks agreement
Why senior people should always speak first on a call
